breadcrumb.name: Inverter Size Calculator for Home Appliances

sections.h2: What size inverter do I need for my home?
p: Add up the running watts of everything that will run on the inverter at the same time, multiply by a safety margin and that is the continuous rating to buy. For the default list of three fans, eight bulbs, a TV, an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC the running load is 1,431 W, the continuous rating 1,789 W and the label rating about 2.24 kVA.

Then check the surge. Motors and compressors draw several times their running watts for a second or two when they start; the inverter's surge or peak rating must cover the running load plus that step. Here the 1 ton inverter AC's step from its running watts to its maximum input is larger than the inverter fridge's, so it sets the surge: 1,731 W. Most inverters quote a surge of about twice their continuous rating, so check the figure on the datasheet, not only the headline kVA.

sections.h2: Can a UPS or inverter run a 1 ton AC?
p: Yes, if it is sized for it. A 1 ton inverter AC runs at about 1,060 W with two fans and has no hard compressor start, so it needs an inverter of about 1,325 W continuous (1.66 kVA) and a surge of 1,360 W. A small home UPS of around one kVA cannot do this; a hybrid or solar inverter of two kVA and up can, as long as its battery bank is big enough for the hours you want.

A 1 ton non-inverter AC is a different matter: its compressor starts at several times its running watts, and most UPS units cannot supply that surge. If the AC is non-inverter, size on the surge figure the calculator shows and expect a much larger inverter.

sections.h2: Inverter for an AC and a fridge together
p: A non-inverter fridge compressor starts at about 1,200 W from 200 W running, and a non-inverter AC compressor at about 3 times its running watts, but only one of them starts in a given instant, so the calculator adds the largest single step, not both. A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with a non-inverter fridge runs at 2,000 W, needs 2,500 W continuous (3.13 kVA) and a surge rating of 5,600 W.
With the inverter models of both appliances the same pair needs far less, which is why a hybrid inverter paired with inverter appliances is the usual recommendation for a solar home.

sections.h2: How many kW of inverter for a home, and what about hybrid inverters?
p: Fans, lights and a TV need under one kW. Add an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC and the home needs about 2.24 kVA; each extra 1.5 ton inverter AC adds roughly one and a half kW of running load. Size for the appliances you will actually run on backup or solar, not for everything in the house, because the inverter cost and the battery it needs grow with the rating.

A hybrid inverter is sized the same way on its AC output side: continuous watts × the margin, with a surge rating for the largest motor. Its solar input side is sized separately from the panels; the solar system calculators cover that. Check that the hybrid inverter's battery voltage matches the battery bank you plan.

faq.q: What size inverter do I need for fans, lights, a fridge and a 1 ton AC?
faq.a: About 1,789 W continuous, or 2.24 kVA, with a surge rating of 1,731 W for the default list on this page (three fans, eight bulbs, a TV, an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC). A non-inverter AC or fridge raises the surge a lot.

faq.q: Can a UPS run a 1 ton AC?
faq.a: A hybrid inverter or large UPS of about two kVA can run a 1 ton inverter AC with a couple of fans (1,325 W continuous, 1,360 W surge). A one kVA home UPS cannot, and a non-inverter AC needs a much larger surge rating. The battery bank decides the hours.

faq.q: How do I calculate inverter capacity from my load?
faq.a: Add the running watts of everything on at once, multiply by the 1.25 margin for the continuous rating, divide by the 0.8 power factor and by one thousand for kVA, then check that the inverter's surge rating covers the running load plus the largest motor's starting step. This calculator does all four steps.

faq.q: What size inverter for an AC and a fridge?
faq.a: A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with a non-inverter fridge runs at 2,000 W but needs a surge rating of 5,600 W, so size on the surge. The inverter versions of both appliances run from a far smaller inverter; see the worked examples.

faq.q: How many kW of inverter does a home need?
faq.a: Fans, lights and a TV alone need under one kW. One inverter AC with a fridge, fans and lights needs about 2.24 kVA, and a home with two 1.5 ton inverter ACs about five to six kVA. Enter your own appliances for the exact figure.

faq.q: Is a hybrid inverter sized differently?
faq.a: No. Its AC output is sized exactly as here: continuous watts × margin and a surge rating for the largest motor. Its solar input and battery voltage are chosen separately; the solar calculators on this site cover them.

faq.q: Does the number of hours change the inverter size?
faq.a: No. Hours decide the battery capacity, not the inverter rating. The inverter must carry the watts whenever the load is on, for one minute or ten hours; the backup time calculator turns hours into battery Ah.

key_facts: Inverter size in watts = the running watts of everything that runs on it at once × a 1.25 safety margin; kVA = watts ÷ a power factor of 0.8 ÷ 1,000.

The surge rating must cover the running load plus the largest single starting step: a non-inverter fridge draws about 1,200 W to start against 200 W running, and a non-inverter AC or water pump about 3 times its running watts for a second or two.
Fans and LED lights alone need a small inverter: 420 W continuous (0.53 kVA) for three fans and eight bulbs; adding a fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC takes it to 1,695 W (2.12 kVA).
A 1.5 ton non-inverter AC with a fridge needs an inverter with a surge rating of 5,600 W although the running load is only 2,000 W; the surge, not the running watts, decides the size.
mistakes: Adding every appliance in the house. Only what runs on the inverter at the same moment counts; an iron or microwave used for minutes is better kept off backup than sized for.

Ignoring the surge. A non-inverter fridge compressor draws about 1,200 W to start and a water pump or non-inverter AC about 3 times its running watts; an inverter sized on running watts alone trips when they start.
Reading VA as watts. An inverter labelled in VA or kVA delivers fewer watts; the calculator converts with a power factor of 0.8 for mixed home loads.
Running the inverter at its limit. The 1.25 margin keeps it cool and leaves room for the phone chargers and extra lights people add later.
Forgetting the battery. The inverter rating sets what you can run; the battery Ah sets for how long. Size the battery with the backup time calculator after this.

examples.title: Fans and lights only
examples.text: Three fans and eight LED bulbs run at 336 W. × 1.25 = 420 W continuous, 0.53 kVA; the fan starting step takes the surge to 376 W. A small home UPS covers this.

examples.title: Fans, lights, an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC
examples.text: Running load 1,356 W, continuous rating 1,695 W (2.12 kVA). Both start softly, but the inverter AC's step up to its maximum input is the larger one, so it sets the surge: 1,656 W.

examples.title: 1.5 ton non-inverter AC and a non-inverter fridge: the surge decides
examples.text: The two run at only 2,000 W, so the continuous rating is 2,500 W (3.13 kVA), but the AC compressor start pushes the surge to 5,600 W. An inverter must carry that peak or it will trip every time the compressor cycles on.

examples.title: Water motor and lights
examples.text: A one hp water motor with six bulbs runs at 1,004 W, so the continuous rating is 1,255 W (1.57 kVA), but the motor starts at about 3 times its running watts and the surge is 2,868 W. Pick an inverter whose peak rating covers it.

examples.title: UPS for a 1 ton inverter AC and two fans
examples.text: Running load 1,060 W, continuous rating 1,325 W, about 1.66 kVA, with a surge of 1,360 W when the AC reaches its maximum input. A two kVA hybrid inverter runs it; the battery bank sets how long.

content.answer: Three fans, eight LED bulbs, a TV, an inverter fridge and a 1 ton inverter AC draw 1,431 W together, so the inverter needs a continuous rating of at least 1,789 W, about 2.24 kVA, with a surge rating of 1,731 W for the AC's step up to full speed, the largest in the list. Inverter watts = running load × margin; kVA = watts ÷ power factor ÷ 1,000.

formula.text: P_run = Σ (W × qty); P_inv = P_run × m; kVA = P_inv ÷ PF ÷ 1000; P_surge = P_run + max(W_start − W)
lines: P_run = total running watts of the appliances on at once
W = running watts of one appliance, qty = how many
m = safety margin on the running load
PF = power factor (converts watts to VA)
P_surge = surge the inverter must supply when the largest motor starts
W_start = starting watts of that motor or compressor

content.safety: Connect an inverter or UPS to house wiring only through a proper changeover so it can never back-feed the grid, use the cable and fuse sizes the maker specifies for the battery side, and have a licensed electrician do the installation.
